paperInfo.subject: Agric, Science & Tech
paperInfo.paperName: Grade 7 Agric, Science & Tech — Paper 2 (Practice Set A)

questions.questionText: SECTION A (30 marks - answer ALL questions in this section, about 75 minutes). Question 1 (5 marks): (a) List any two environmental factors that affect agriculture [2]. (b) Describe any one branch of agriculture [1]. (c) Give one profession in agriculture [1]. (d) Which department deals with crop protection (pests and diseases) in agriculture? [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Two environmental factors affecting agriculture:** **rainfall amount/distribution** and **air temperature** (also valid: **soil type/fertility, wind speed, relief/topography, altitude, and relative humidity**) [2 marks]. **(b) Description of one branch of agriculture:** **Animal Husbandry**—the scientific branch of agriculture focused on breeding, feeding, housing, and caring for domestic farm animals (cattle, goats, sheep, pigs, poultry) to yield meat, milk, eggs, hides, and draught power (or *Crop Husbandry / Soil Science / Agricultural Engineering / Agricultural Economics*) [1 mark]. **(c) One agricultural profession:** **Veterinarian** (animal doctor), **AGRITEX Agricultural Extension Officer**, **Agronomist**, or **Soil Scientist** [1 mark]. **(d) Crop protection department:** **Plant Protection / Research & Specialist Services (Crop Protection / Plant Quarantine Services)** handles crop pests and plant disease control [1 mark].

Environmental climate governs almost every regional farming pattern across Zimbabwe: cool misty Eastern Highlands (**Natural Region I**) suit tea, timber, and apples cleanly, whereas hot dry lowveld **Natural Region V** relies on hardy drought-tolerant sorghum, cattle ranching, or irrigated sugar cane!

Always make sure parts (b), (c), and (d) answer precisely what is asked: a **Branch** is a broad field of work (*Agronomy/Animal Husbandry*), a **Profession** is a trained job title (*Agronomist/Vet*), and the **Department** is the specialist protection unit (**Plant Protection**).

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a) Name two agents of physical (mechanical) weathering [2]. (b) What do the following terms mean: (i) soil fertility [1]; (ii) soil erosion [1]. (c) How does crop rotation improve soil fertility? [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Two agents of physical (mechanical) weathering:** **daily temperature fluctuations** (heating rocks hot by day so outer layers expand, then chilling cold at night so shells crack like onion skin—*exfoliation*), **water/ice frost wedging** inside rock cracks, **wind-blown sand abrasion**, and **prying plant tree roots** splitting crevices [2 marks]. **(b)(i) Soil fertility:** the natural capacity of soil to supply balanced essential **plant mineral nutrients, adequate water, and air** to support healthy vigorous crop growth [1 mark]. **(ii) Soil erosion:** the physical loosening, **washing away by running water, or blowing away by strong wind** of valuable fertile upper **topsoil** [1 mark]. **(c) How crop rotation improves fertility:** rotating heavy-feeding cereals (maize) with nitrogen-fixing **legumes** (beans, groundnuts, cowpeas) allows *Rhizobium* root bacteria to trap fresh atmospheric **nitrogen**, while alternating root depths recycles balanced minerals cleanly without exhausting one soil layer [1 mark].

Notice the key distinction between **physical weathering**—breaking giant solid rocks into smaller mineral gravel *without* altering rock chemistry—and **chemical weathering** (like weak rainwater acid dissolving limestone minerals).

In part (b), keep **(i) Soil fertility (supplying nutrients/moisture/air for plant growth)** cleanly separated from **(ii) Soil erosion (physical removal/loss of fertile topsoil)**—never mix up nutrient exhaustion with physical washing away!

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a)(i) A rain gauge recorded the following monthly rainfall: January 45mm, February 60mm, March 35mm, April 20mm. Calculate the total rainfall for these four months [2]. (ii) Which instrument is used to measure rainfall? [1]. (b) What measures should a farmer take to protect crops against hailstorm damage? [2]
questions.explanation:
**Worked Solution & Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a)(i) Total rainfall calculation:** Add all four monthly rainfall measurements carefully step by step: **January 45 mm + February 60 mm = 105 mm**; next add **March 35 mm → 105 + 35 = 140 mm**; finally add **April 20 mm → 140 + 20 = 160 mm** (**Total 4-month rainfall = 160 mm**) [2 marks]. **(ii) Rainfall instrument:** **Rain gauge** (mounted level in open ground away from tall trees/buildings, measured using a calibrated measuring cylinder in millimetres) [1 mark]. **(b) Two hailstorm protection measures:** stretching protective **hail-shade netting** over high-value garden/nursery beds or growing tender produce inside greenhouses, alongside timing planting or choosing **quick-maturing/sturdy varieties** and taking out **hail crop insurance** [2 marks].

Looking at these monthly totals (**45, 60, 35, 20 mm** totalling only **160 mm** across peak January–April!) immediately alerts an agronomist to severe dry-season moisture deficit—proving why soil mulching and drought-hardy small grains (*sorghum/cowpeas*) become vital here!

Check your arithmetic column-by-column twice (**5 + 0 + 5 + 0 = 10**, write 0 carry 1; **1 + 4 + 6 + 3 + 2 = 16 → 160 mm**) and always write the exact **mm** unit beside the final number!

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a) What are pesticides? [1]. (b) Why should a farmer wear protective clothing when applying agro-chemicals? [2]. (c) What do the following colour codes on agro-chemical containers mean: (i) red [1]; (ii) blue? [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of pesticides:** Synthetic or natural **chemical substances manufactured specifically to repel, control, or kill harmful pests**—including insects (*insecticides*), crop weeds (*herbicides*), fungal rots (*fungicides*), or rats (*rodenticides*) [1 mark]. **(b) Two reasons for protective clothing (PPE):** waterproof gloves, masks, goggles, overalls, and boots shield permeable **skin, eyes, and delicate lungs** from toxic chemical droplets or mist, preventing acute **chemical skin burns, eye blindness, and internal poisoning** [2 marks]. **(c) Hazard label triangle colour codes:** **(i) Red triangle:** warns the agrochemical is **very toxic / highly poisonous** requiring extreme caution, locked storage, and full respirator PPE [1 mark]; **(ii) Blue (or Amber) code:** signals **moderately hazardous** toxicity—still dangerous enough to demand full protective clothing, careful label dosing, and strict child exclusion [1 mark]. *(Note: On official Zimbabwe agrochemical triangles, colours step upward cleanly from **Green = Caution / Slightly Toxic → Amber = Moderately Toxic → Red = Very Toxic → Purple = Extremely Poisonous**; some regional/WHO classifications also mark Class II/III strips in Blue as moderately hazardous.)*

Reading the hazard triangle AND obeying the **Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI)** protects not just the sprayer operator in the field, but also innocent consumers eating farm tomatoes days later!

Name actual concrete routes of body entry (**skin absorption, eye splash, lung inhalation**) blocked by PPE rather than vaguely saying *"to stay clean"*.

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a) What is malnutrition? [1]. (b) State one function of each of the following nutrients: (i) fats [1]; (ii) vitamins [1]. (c) Give one disease caused by a lack of: (i) vitamin C [1]; (ii) protein [1]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of malnutrition:** A health disorder arising from eating an **unbalanced diet**—either **undernutrition** (too little food or severe shortage of specific nutrients like protein or vitamins) or excessive over-consumption causing obesity [1 mark]. **(b)(i) Function of fats:** fats supply a highly **concentrated store of slow-release body energy**, insulate vital organs against cold, and carry essential **fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)** cleanly into the body [1 mark]. **(ii) Function of vitamins:** vital **protective micronutrients** that strengthen the immune system against infections, promote wound healing, keep night vision sharp, and regulate healthy cell growth [1 mark]. **(c) Deficiency diseases:** **(i) Lack of Vitamin C causes Scurvy** (bleeding swollen gums, slow wound healing, sore joints) [1 mark]; **(ii) Severe lack of Protein causes Kwashiorkor** (swollen belly/feet oedema, reddish thin hair, slow growth in children) [1 mark].

Notice why smallholder kitchen gardens growing fresh **spinach, covo, tomatoes, pawpaws, and beans** defeat malnutrition effortlessly right at home: leafy greens and citrus fruits supply Vitamin C stopping scurvy, while beans, groundnuts, eggs, and milk furnish crisp plant/animal protein curing kwashiorkor!

Double-check spelling accurately in Paper 2: **Scurvy** (*Vitamin C deficiency*), **Kwashiorkor** (*Protein deficiency*), **Rickets** (*Vitamin D/Calcium*), and **Goitre** (*Iodine*)!

questions.questionText: (5 marks): (a) State whether the price will be high or low in the following situations: (i) many bananas but few buyers [1]; (ii) few eggs and many buyers [1]. (b) Give one advantage of growing tomatoes under irrigation in the dry season [1]. (c) Give any two disadvantages of using very old farm machinery [2]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a)(i) Many bananas, few buyers → Price will be LOW:** heavy market **excess supply (glut)** exceeding limited buyer **demand** forces traders to slash prices sharply so perishable bananas sell before rotting black [1 mark]. **(ii) Few eggs, many buyers → Price will be HIGH:** acute **scarcity** paired with intense shopper competition allows farmers/sellers to charge **premium higher prices** [1 mark]. **(b) Advantage of dry-season irrigated tomatoes:** irrigating winter/dry-season tomatoes lets a grower harvest bright red trays during months when rainfed growers have **zero competing supply**, earning top scarce market prices and high profit margins [1 mark]. **(c) Two disadvantages of very old farm machinery:** worn-out tractors and pumps suffer **frequent costly breakdowns** during critical planting windows (delaying fieldwork), consume excessive **fuel/oil inefficiently**, require scarce expensive **spare parts**, and lack modern protective **safety guards** [2 marks].

Understanding basic **Supply and Demand** turns farmers into strategic marketers: instead of planting cabbages or tomatoes simultaneously with every neighbour in summer, staggering cold-season irrigated crops captures lush prices calmly!

Show both **Supply vs Demand price direction** AND **why perishable dry-season irrigation beats glut markets**, naming two distinct tractor drawbacks (**breakdown delays + high fuel/repair costs**).

questions.questionText: SECTION B (20 marks - answer any TWO of questions 7 to 10, about 45 minutes). Question 7 (about 10 marks): (a) Complete a table on causes of plant damage and their control, for: (i) veld fires; (ii) pests; (iii) waterlogging [3]. (b) What are the effects of the following on crops: (i) diseases [2]; (ii) drought? [2]. (c) Describe three ways of controlling soil erosion in a crop field [3]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [10 marks]:** **(a) Plant damage & control:** **(i) Veld fires:** prevent by slashing/ploughing **clean perimeter firebreaks (fireguards)** before dry windy months, banning reckless grass burning, and suppressing sparks rapidly [1 mark]; **(ii) Crop pests:** manage using **crop rotation, resistant varieties, natural biological predators, and targeted approved pesticides** [1 mark]; **(iii) Waterlogging:** prevent by digging open **drainage channels/cut-off drains**, shaping **raised beds/ridges**, and avoiding wasteful over-irrigation [1 mark]. **(b) Crop impacts:** **(i) Plant diseases:** fungi, bacteria, and viruses destroy leaves/roots, **stunt growth, slash harvest quantity, blemish market quality** (rotting tomatoes/potatoes), or kill entire plants [2 marks]; **(ii) Drought:** severe soil moisture deficit causes **poor uneven germination, leaf wilting, failed maize pollination/barren ears, stunted yields, or complete crop failure** [2 marks]. **(c) Three erosion-control methods in crop fields:** building gentle **contour ridges**, mulching bare soil with dry **grass/stover** to block raindrop splash, and practising **minimum tillage (Pfumvudza basins) / planting cover crops or grass buffer strips** along slopes [3 marks].

Observe how physical hazards (veld fires, waterlogging, soil wash) and biological threats (diseases, insects) reinforce each other when neglected—for instance, waterlogged weak roots quickly rot under fungal soil diseases!

Answer all sub-parts cleanly using numbered sub-headings (a)(i)-(iii), (b)(i)-(ii), and (c) matching mark weights cleanly—never compress a 10-mark Section B answer into two casual sentences!

questions.questionText: (about 10-11 marks): (a) Describe five ways of preventing diseases in farm animals [5]. (b) What is an infectious disease? [1]. (c) Describe one infectious disease of farm animals under the following headings: (i) name of disease [1]; (ii) symptoms [2]; (iii) measures for controlling the disease [2]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [11 marks]:** **(a) Five ways to prevent livestock diseases:** **(1) Routine timely vaccinations** before seasonal outbreaks; **(2) Strictly quarantining newly purchased stock** (2–4 weeks) and immediately isolating sick animals; **(3) Sweeping, drying, and disinfecting kraals/fowl runs** alongside clean feeders/drinkers; **(4) Feeding clean balanced diets and fresh water** to keep strong natural immunity; and **(5) Regular dipping/spraying** to kill disease-carrying ticks and flies (plus avoiding stressful overcrowding) [5 marks]. **(b) Definition of infectious disease:** A contagious sickness caused by harmful living **micro-organisms or parasites (bacteria, viruses, protozoa)** that **spreads rapidly from sick animals to healthy animals** via air, saliva, droppings, bites, or dirty equipment [1 mark]. **(c) Profiled infectious disease — Foot-and-Mouth Disease (FMD):** **(i) Name:** Foot-and-Mouth Disease [1 mark]; **(ii) Symptoms:** painful **fluid blisters/ulcers inside mouth, tongue, and between cloven hooves**, heavy stringy **drooling/salivation**, severe **lameness**, high fever, and sudden drop in eating/milk [2 marks]; **(iii) Control measures:** enforce strict **livestock quarantine and zero cattle movement bans**, disinfect boots/tyres/trucks, vaccinate surrounding buffer herds, and **report suspected cases immediately to veterinary authorities** [2 marks].

Foot-and-Mouth Disease carries national quarantine importance across Zimbabwe because a single hidden outbreak shuts down beef export markets and communal cattle sales across whole provinces!

Make sure you keep **(b) Infectious disease** strictly focused on **spread from animal to animal by pathogens**—unlike non-infectious mineral deficiencies (*milk fever*) or physical broken legs!

questions.questionText: (about 10 marks): (a) Describe the following: (i) afforestation [1]; (ii) deforestation [1]. (b) Describe the establishment of a woodlot under the following headings: (i) site selection [3]; (ii) planting [2]; (iii) maintenance/care of young trees [3]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [10 marks]:** **(a) Forestry terms:** **(i) Afforestation:** planting young trees purposefully to establish a **brand-new forest or farm woodlot on bare land that did not carry woodland previously** [1 mark]; **(ii) Deforestation:** **reckless large-scale cutting down and clearing of natural trees/forests** without matching replanting, leaving slopes exposed [1 mark]. **(b) Woodlot establishment steps:** **(i) Site selection [3 marks]:** pick deep, well-drained soil matched to eucalyptus/pine/indigenous species, close to **reliable water** for nursery watering yet away from swampy waterlogged bottoms or rocky gullies, with clear **road access** for hauling future poles [3 marks]; **(ii) Planting [2 marks]:** prepare clean **60×60 cm holes** spaced neatly (e.g. 2 m × 2 m) right as **steady summer rains start**, loosen plastic sleeves carefully without shattering root-balls, plant level, firm soil gently, and **water immediately** [2 marks]; **(iii) Maintenance [3 marks]:** ring-weed cleanly around young saplings so wild grass doesn’t choke light/water, water during dry first-year spells, **mulch bases, fence out browsing goats/cattle, plough clean perimeter firebreaks**, and **beat up (replant)** any dead gaps promptly [3 marks].

Remember that planting during dry winter dust kills almost every un-irrigated seedling within weeks—matching planting straight into soaked November/December rains boosts woodlot survival above 90%!

Examiners check specifically whether you distinguish **Afforestation (new woodland on previously treeless land)** vs **Reforestation (replanting land where forest was cut/burned)** vs **Deforestation (destructive clearing)**!

questions.questionText: (10 marks): A farmer recorded the following business activities in a season: Bought 30kg of vegetable seed for $90; Bought 8 bags of fertiliser at $25 each; Bought chemicals for $45; Sold 800 bundles of vegetables at $2 for 5 bundles; Sold 12 bags of 50kg maize at $18 each. (a) Calculate the total expenses [3]. (b) Calculate the total returns (income) [3]. (c) Calculate the profit or loss made by the farmer [2]. (d) Give two advantages of a farmer selling produce directly to consumers rather than through a middleman [2]
questions.explanation:
**Worked Financial Solution [10 marks]:** **(a) Total Expenses calculation:** Sum every farm purchase carefully line by line:
- Vegetable seed = **$90.00**
- Fertiliser = 8 bags × $25.00/bag = **$200.00**
- Chemicals = **$45.00**
- **Total Expenses = $90 + $200 + $45 = $335.00** [3 marks].
**(b) Total Returns (Income) calculation:** Compute each crop enterprise revenue carefully:
- Vegetables: 800 bundles sold in groups of 5 bundles at $2.00 per lot → **800 ÷ 5 = 160 lots** → **160 × $2.00 = $320.00**
- Maize: 12 bags × $18.00/bag = **$216.00**
- **Total Returns (Income) = $320 + $216 = $536.00** [3 marks].
**(c) Profit or Loss calculation:** Because Total Returns (**$536.00**) exceed Total Expenses (**$335.00**), the farm achieved a **Net Profit**: **$536.00 − $335.00 = $201.00 PROFIT** [2 marks].

**(d) Two advantages of direct selling over middlemen:** First, selling straight at farm gates or community stalls lets the farmer **keep the full retail price ($100%)** instead of surrendering steep wholesale **commission/mark-up discounts** to intermediaries [1 mark]; second, the farmer receives **instant prompt cash on delivery**, builds loyal repeat customers who trust freshness, and keeps sharper control over pricing and produce feedback [1 mark].

Notice how showing the vegetable grouping cleanly (**800 ÷ 5 = 160 lots × $2 = $320**) prevents the classic student error of multiplying 800 × $2 = $1,600! Always double-check unit ratios ("$2 per 5 bundles") and state **"PROFIT"** explicitly beside **$201.00**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer notices that the topsoil is being washed away after heavy rain.
- (a) Name the process taking place. [1 mark]
- (b) State two causes of the problem. [2 marks]
- (c) Give two methods of controlling it. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Process taking place:** **Soil erosion** (specifically sheet/raindrop-splash water erosion stripping fertile upper topsoil across bare slopes) [1 mark]. **(b) Two causes of the problem:** heavy torrential rainfall striking exposed, bare unmulched soil directly, plus poor land practices such as **overgrazing, deforestation, or ploughing straight up and down slopes** rather than across contours [2 marks]. **(c) Two methods of controlling it:** building graded **contour ridges / contour ploughing** across the slope to intercept runoff, and applying **organic grass mulch or planting cover grass/vetiver strips** to shield topsoil and bind crumbs with roots [2 marks].

Soil erosion destroys farm productivity fastest because topsoil—holding nearly all dark organic humus, beneficial earthworms, nitrogen, and water-absorbing crumbs—lies only in the top 15–20 cm above sterile subsoil or bedrock. Once naked soil loses vegetation cover, pounding raindrops break soil aggregates apart, sealing surface pores so rainwater rushes swiftly down tracks and carves shallow sheet wash into deep unstoppable gullies.

In ZIMSEC Grade 7 Agriculture & Science Paper 2, do not merely name *"trees"* vaguely when asked for control methods—state actionable techniques cleanly (**ploughing along the contour**, **mulching bare inter-rows**, **terracing**, **planting vetiver grass strips**, or **rotational grazing**).

questions.questionText:
A school starts a compost heap using crop residues and kitchen waste.
- (a) Define compost. [1 mark]
- (b) State two materials that can be composted. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why water is added during compost making. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of compost:** Well-decomposed, dark, crumbly **organic fertiliser** formed naturally when plant residues, dry grass, kitchen vegetable wastes, and small amounts of manure rot down steadily under controlled moisture and air [1 mark]. **(b) Two compostable materials:** dry maize stalks/grass (*carbon-rich "brown" matter*) paired with green vegetable peelings, weeds before flowering, or kraal/poultry manure (*nitrogen-rich "green" activators*) [2 marks]. **(c) Why water is added:** Essential moisture activates and sustains **decomposer micro-organisms (beneficial bacteria and fungi)** inside the heap so they multiply rapidly, digest tough plant fibres into rich humus, and regulate healthy fermentation warmth [2 marks].

A properly layered compost heap relies on living microscopic decomposers that work just like tiny soil farmers: if the heap turns bone-dry, bacteria stop breaking stems down completely, whereas soaking it soggy drowns oxygen air pockets and turns the pile smelly and anaerobic! Sprinkling water gently like a **wrung-out damp sponge** and turning every 3–4 weeks balances air, warmth (~55–65°C inside), and moisture smoothly.

Examiners check specifically that you state **living micro-organisms / bacteria / fungi need moisture to survive and break down the waste**, and remind farmers never to toss **meat scraps, cooking oil, glass, plastics, or thick diseased twigs** onto garden compost heaps.

questions.questionText:
A farmer grows maize and keeps cattle on the same farm.
- (a) Name the type of farming enterprise involving both crops and livestock. [1 mark]
- (b) Give two benefits of integrating crops and livestock. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain how manure can support crop production. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Type of farming enterprise:** **Mixed farming** (raising crops and domesticated farm livestock together in one integrated farm unit) [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits of integrating crops and livestock:** spreading household financial and drought **risk across multiple income sources** (selling milk or goats if maize prices dip), plus building a **self-feeding biological cycle** where dried maize stover, sorghum stalks, and garden trimmings become cheap winter cattle feed while cattle/goat manure enriches crop fields [2 marks]. **(c) How manure supports crop production:** cured livestock manure returns essential plant macronutrients (**nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium**) and trace minerals while adding spongy **organic humus** that loosens heavy clay, thickens light sandy water storage, and boosts harvest yields [2 marks].

Smallholder mixed farms in Zimbabwe remain far more resilient than pure monocrop farms because cattle pull ox-ploughs for timely planting in November, provide fresh milk daily, and convert tough inedible crop stalks into dark soil-building manure without buying expensive imported bags every season.

Keep distinct **Mixed Farming** (both crops and livestock deliberately integrated on the same farm) versus **Monoculture** (repeatedly growing one single crop species across fields season after season).

questions.questionText:
A farmer plans to irrigate vegetables during a dry period.
- (a) Name one irrigation method. [1 mark]
- (b) State two advantages of irrigation. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain one risk of poor irrigation management. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Named irrigation method:** **Drip irrigation** (delivering slow water drops cleanly straight to each plant root), **sprinkler irrigation**, or **furrow/basin irrigation** [1 mark]. **(b) Two advantages of irrigation:** frees farmers from total reliance on unpredictable rains by permitting **year-round winter and off-season cropping**, and protects tall yields reliably against destructive mid-season dry spells [2 marks]. **(c) One risk of poor irrigation management:** **over-irrigating poorly drained soils** causes **waterlogging** (driving life-giving oxygen out of root air spaces so roots suffocate and rot), **leaches soluble nitrogen fertilisers** below active roots, and spreads fungal soil diseases [2 marks].

Comparing methods smartly matters too: **drip irrigation** saves up to 50% more scarce borehole water than overhead sprinklers during windy afternoons because drops soak directly at shaded plant bases without evaporating mid-air or wetting foliage with fungal spores.

Always match the irrigation fault to its exact consequence in Paper 2: **too much water → waterlogging + root oxygen starvation + nutrient leaching**; **using salty/dirty water → soil salinisation or crop contamination**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer keeps dairy cattle.
- (a) What is dairy farming? [1 mark]
- (b) State two requirements for healthy dairy cattle. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why clean water is important. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of dairy farming:** Keeping specialised cattle breeds (such as **Holstein-Friesian, Jersey, Guernsey, or Mashona/crossbred dairy cows**) primarily for clean, high-volume **milk production** and dairy products [1 mark]. **(b) Two requirements for healthy dairy cattle:** supplying abundant **balanced, high-protein/energy rations** (lush pasture/napier fodder plus dairy meal concentrates) alongside **clean, shaded, mud-free housing, gentle hygiene at milking, and routine dipping/vaccinations** [2 marks]. **(c) Importance of clean water:** fresh milk is **~87% water**, so lactating cows must drink huge daily volumes (**50–90+ litres per cow daily**) of clean fresh water to synthesise milk cleanly, cool body heat, digest rough dry hay, and prevent waterborne scours or mastitis contamination [2 marks].

Even a top-pedigree Holstein cow eating expensive dairy concentrates drops litres sharply within 24 hours if troughs run empty or sit slimy and stagnant—water is literally the single highest-volume nutrient in a milk bucket!

In ZIMSEC answers on dairy nutrition, quoting that **milk is roughly 85–87% water** makes your biological reason immediately airtight and earns full marks effortlessly.

questions.questionText:
A crop is attacked by insects.
- (a) Define a pest. [1 mark]
- (b) Name two methods of pest control. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why integrated pest management can be useful. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of a pest:** Any living organism—including biting/sucking **insects, mites, nematodes, rodents (rats), grain-eating birds, competing weeds, or disease fungi**—that damages crops, feeds on stored harvests, or lowers agricultural yield and quality [1 mark]. **(b) Two pest-control methods:** targeted **chemical control** (applying safe approved insecticides/fungicides cleanly) alongside **biological control** (encouraging natural predators like ladybirds eating aphids) or **cultural rotation and hand-picking** [2 marks]. **(c) Value of Integrated Pest Management (IPM):** combining preventive cultural sanitation, mechanical traps, biological predators, and sparing last-resort chemicals slashes spraying **costs**, prevents pests from evolving **chemical resistance**, protects friendly **honeybees/pollinators**, and reduces toxic food residues [2 marks].

Think of IPM as defending a fortress in layers: resistant crop seeds and clean weeded edges stop pests from settling first, natural predators guard plants daily, and careful targeted sprays step in only when pest counts cross real economic danger levels.

Never define pests narrowly as *"bad bugs"* only—remember ZIMSEC includes **insects, rodents, weeds, birds, and pathogens** as crop pests whenever they harm agricultural productivity.

questions.questionText:
A farmer wants to improve soil fertility.
- (a) Name one organic manure. [1 mark]
- (b) State two benefits of organic manure. [2 marks]
- (c) Give one precaution when handling manure. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Named organic manure:** **Kraal (cattle/goat) manure, poultry droppings, or garden compost** [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits of organic manure:** rebuilds dark spongy **organic humus** that loosens sticky clay and boosts moisture retention in dry sand, while steadily feeding crops with slow-release balanced macronutrients and trace minerals at almost zero cash cost [2 marks]. **(c) Precaution when handling manure:** ensure fresh raw manure (especially hot concentrated chicken droppings!) is **properly rotted/cured** before touching tender vegetable seedlings so soluble ammonia does not scorch delicate roots, and **wash hands thoroughly with soap** after handling dung [1 mark].

Unlike quick mineral fertilisers that dissolve overnight and leach down fast during storms, dark cured organic manure nourishes soil earthworms and beneficial microbes that glue fine dust particles into airy water-holding soil crumbs lasting several seasons.

Notice the twin handling precautions examiners expect: **(1) curing raw dung so heat/ammonia doesn't burn young plants** AND **(2) personal soap hygiene (plus avoiding spreading raw manure onto ready-to-eat raw salad leaves!)**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer stores harvested grain for several months.
- (a) State one condition required for safe grain storage. [1 mark]
- (b) Name two storage pests or problems. [2 marks]
- (c) Give two ways of reducing storage losses. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Condition for safe grain storage:** harvested maize, sorghum, or beans must first be **dried thoroughly down to low moisture (~12–12.5%)** and kept inside a **cool, dry, waterproof, well-ventilated, pest-sealed granary or store** [1 mark]. **(b) Two storage pests/problems:** destructive boring insects like **maize weevils (*Sitophilus*) and Larger Grain Borer (*Prostephanus*)**, **rodents/rats**, and toxic **storage moulds** (*Aspergillus* producing poisons) [2 marks]. **(c) Two ways to reduce storage losses:** storing spotless dry grain inside **airtight hermetic bags (e.g. PICS bags) or sealed metal silos** that suffocate insects without poison, or cleaning/dusting empty granaries cleanly, sealing rat-gaps, and applying approved grain protectant dusts on bags stacked on raised **wooden pallets** [2 marks].

Smallholder farmers often lose up to a third of hard-won grain between May and December solely from rushing slightly damp cobs into old dusty cribs—simply testing dryness cleanly ("teeth bite crack test" or salt-jar check) saves whole sacks from rotting silently.

Include both **physical/structural protection (dry ≤ 12% moisture, pallets off damp floors, clean stores)** and **pest exclusion (hermetic bags, safe grain protectants, rat traps/guards)**.

questions.questionText:
A herd of cattle is grazing continuously in one small area.
- (a) Name the problem that may result. [1 mark]
- (b) State two effects of overgrazing. [2 marks]
- (c) Suggest two grazing-management measures. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Problem resulting:** **Overgrazing** (stocking too many grazing animals continuously onto one small paddock faster than pasture grass can regrow reserves) [1 mark]. **(b) Two effects of overgrazing:** sweet nutritious grass species get bitten down to bare roots and die out (replaced by tough unpalatable thorn scrub), leaving bare compacted trampled earth swept swiftly into **severe sheet and gully soil erosion** during summer storms [2 marks]. **(c) Two grazing-management measures:** dividing pastures into fenced **rotational grazing paddocks** so each grazed block enjoys long recovery rest while stock graze fresh blocks, and balancing herd size cleanly to the land’s **carrying capacity** (supplementing winter herds with hay/stover instead of starving veld bare) [2 marks].

Grass plants store energy in underground roots: continuous close nibbling every day drains root reserves completely so plants starve, whereas letting grass rest after short grazing turns paddocks thicker and deeper-rooted every rainy season.

Link **continuous grazing on one small area → overgrazing → loss of palatable grasses + exposed compacted soil → erosion**, and give concrete fixes (**rotational grazing paddocks**, **matching carrying capacity**).

questions.questionText:
A farmer wants to reduce livestock disease.
- (a) Name one disease-prevention measure. [1 mark]
- (b) State two hygiene practices. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain the value of vaccination. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Named disease-prevention measure:** **Timely vaccination, routine tick dipping/spraying, or strict quarantine of new/sick stock** [1 mark]. **(b) Two hygiene practices:** regularly sweeping, scrubbing, and **disinfecting livestock kraals, pens, and footbaths**, alongside supplying spotless **clean feeding troughs and fresh drinkers** free of manure droppings [2 marks]. **(c) Value of vaccination:** vaccines introduce safe harmless/weakened germs into healthy animals **before** outbreaks strike, stimulating the animal’s immune system to produce protective **antibodies** against deadly killers like **Newcastle Disease, Anthrax, or Blackleg** [2 marks].

Remember that vaccination works strictly as a *shield for healthy animals*—waiting until half the fowl run is dying to buy vaccines wastes money because antibodies take 10–14 days to build up safely.

Keep sharp clarity between **Vaccination (builds preventive immunity in healthy animals beforehand)** versus **Antibiotics (treats bacterial infections only after sickness strikes)**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer uses a knapsack sprayer.
- (a) State one use of a knapsack sprayer. [1 mark]
- (b) Name two safety precautions. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain why chemical labels must be followed. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Use of a knapsack sprayer:** **Applying carefully diluted liquid pesticides (insecticides/fungicides), weed-killing herbicides, or liquid foliar fertilisers** evenly over crops [1 mark]. **(b) Two safety precautions:** wearing full **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)** (impermeable gloves, face mask/respirator, goggles, overalls, and gumboots) and **never spraying into facing wind** (nor eating, drinking, or smoking while handling chemicals) [2 marks]. **(c) Why chemical labels must be followed:** labels state exact safe **mixing dilution rates** (avoiding poisonous residues or crop leaf scorch), specific target pests, PPE warnings, and mandatory **Pre-Harvest Intervals (PHIs)** telling farmers how many days to wait safely before picking food [2 marks].

Spraying early morning or late calm evening protects beneficial honeybees (which forage during sunny midday hours) while ensuring fine chemical droplets settle neatly onto leaves rather than blowing straight back into the farmer’s eyes.

Never give thin advice like *"be careful"*—state concrete **PPE items (mask, gloves, goggles, boots)**, **wind direction rule**, and exact **label reasons (dilution + Pre-Harvest Interval + poisoning avoidance)**.

questions.questionText:
A farm manager keeps records of sales, inputs and expenses.
- (a) Name the management practice. [1 mark]
- (b) State two benefits of farm records. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain how records help decision-making. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Management practice:** **Farm record keeping** (maintaining written/digital physical production and financial transaction books systematically) [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits of farm records:** proves accurately whether each enterprise earned a **net profit or cash loss**, while tracking daily **feed/fertiliser usage, animal vaccinations, calving dates, and missing tools/theft** [2 marks]. **(c) How records help decision-making:** comparing past seasonal records spotlights the highest-earning enterprises vs money-losing crops, supports realistic **next-season budgets**, spots pest/disease timings early, and provides solid proof banks inspect before approving **agricultural credit loans** [2 marks].

Memory tricks every farmer into remembering peak harvests while forgetting dozens of small mid-season cash leaks—written ledgers make quiet small expenses visible on one page.

Separate clearly **production records** (yields, rainfall, mortalities) from **financial records** (receipts, costs, profit), and highlight **budgeting + enterprise comparison + bank loans**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer wants to reduce financial risk.
- (a) Define risk in farming. [1 mark]
- (b) State two ways of reducing risk. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain the value of diversification. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Risk in farming:** **Unpredictable uncertain hazards**—such as sudden drought, hailstorms, armyworm outbreaks, foot-and-mouth disease, or sharp market price drops—that can ruin yields or cause serious financial loss [1 mark]. **(b) Two ways of reducing risk:** spreading production across **enterprise diversification**, buying **agricultural crop/livestock insurance**, or investing in **irrigation and staggered planting dates** [2 marks]. **(c) Value of diversification:** raising several independent enterprises together (for instance **maize + sugar beans + goats + broilers**) means that if drought hits maize or tomato market prices crash, steady goat and egg cash still buys family food and covers farm debts [2 marks].

"Never put all your eggs in one basket" holds especially true under rainfed Zimbabwean skies: mixing hardy drought-tolerant small grains with deep-rooted crops and hardy indigenous livestock shields homesteads against single-event shocks.

Differentiate clearly between **avoiding risk before planting (diversification, irrigation, drought-hardy varieties)** and **transferring financial loss (insurance, savings reserves)**.

questions.questionText:
A farmer selects healthy seeds before planting.
- (a) State one characteristic of good seed. [1 mark]
- (b) Give two reasons for using good seed. [2 marks]
- (c) State one condition needed for germination. [1 mark]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [4 marks]:** **(a) Characteristic of good seed:** **High germination percentage (>85–90%)**, plumb clean unwrinkled size, pure true-to-variety identity, and **complete freedom from weevil holes, rot, weed seeds, and seed-borne disease spores** [1 mark]. **(b) Two reasons for using good seed:** delivers **fast uniform vigorous seedling emergence** capturing early rains and shading weeds out cleanly (raising final yield), while preventing farmers from accidentally planting dangerous **parasitic weed seeds or blight germs** into fresh soil [2 marks]. **(c) Condition needed for germination:** sufficient **water/moisture** to soften seed coats and activate enzymes, paired with adequate **warmth** and **oxygen air** for seed respiration [1 mark].

Testing saved or bought seed a month early by wrapping 20 seeds inside a damp cloth/paper towel for 7 days reveals true **germination %** cheaply—saving farmers from wasting basal fertiliser beneath dead seed!

Never write *"sunlight"* as one of the three classic germination conditions in Grade 7 science/agriculture—almost all crop seeds germinate underground in total darkness given **Water + Oxygen + Suitable Warmth**!

questions.questionText:
A farmer uses crop rotation.
- (a) Define crop rotation. [1 mark]
- (b) State two benefits. [2 marks]
- (c) Explain how rotation can help manage pests or fertility. [2 marks]
questions.explanation:
**Model Answer [5 marks]:** **(a) Definition of crop rotation:** Growing **different crop families in a planned, recurring seasonal sequence** across divided farm plots rather than planting the same crop repeatedly on one patch [1 mark]. **(b) Two benefits:** disrupts specialist **soil pests and plant diseases**, balances extraction of **mineral nutrients at varied rooting depths**, and suppresses host-specific weeds like witchweed (*Striga*) [2 marks]. **(c) How rotation helps pests or fertility:** including **legumes** (groundnuts, cowpeas, beans) allows *Rhizobium* bacteria in root nodules to **fix free atmospheric nitrogen** into fertile nitrates for demanding maize next year, while switching botanical families starves specialist root nematodes and blights between host seasons [2 marks].

Remember that a genuine rotation rotates **botanical plant families** cleanly—e.g. **Cereal (Maize) → Legume (Beans) → Root/Leaf (Sweet Potato/Cabbages)**—because planting tomatoes straight after potatoes fails to break blight or nematode cycles!

Score maximum marks by explicitly naming **Rhizobium nitrogen fixation in legume root nodules** AND **breaking host-specific soil pest/disease cycles**.
